<meta>Continuity: Continues the discussion of late Kāngrā and Garhwāl painting, moving toward a broader discussion of how Rajput painting functioned as a traditional, non-individualistic art form compared to modern Western art.</meta>

Sometimes half-finished works are more impressive than the finished picture. However, when comparing these, one sees that completing a work by a master’s hand does not necessarily involve the slightest loss of inspiration. These two examples, along with others—such as Plates LIII, LIV, A, and many more not illustrated here—perfectly demonstrate how the same subject can be treated repeatedly without becoming monotonous. There is a close analogy between the set theme of a picture and the set form of a <term>rāga</term> (a melodic framework in Indian music); in each case, a skeleton—or as the Indians say, the "trunk of the tree"—is provided, and each artist must add the leaves and branches himself. Just as no song is ever exactly repeated, neither is any picture; instead, each fresh rendering is closely related to the others. This theory of art differs entirely from the modern conception of professional art, where each subject treated by a master is considered "finished" once and for all. In the modern view, no other artist dares to tackle the same subject for fear of being accused of plagiarism or lack of originality. This leads one to mistakenly think of art as a treasury of masterpieces created by men of exceptional genius. In contrast, Hindu art—both formal (hieratic) and folk (vernacular)—has always been more or less a national art, driven by the desire to have certain groups of ideas constantly re-presented.

The Rājasthānī and Pahāṛī areas are divided by the Punjab plains, stretching from Delhi to Lahore. During the Mughal period, this region contributed little to art because the energy of the Mughal influence was directed toward glorifying the royal court, and the life of that court had little to do with the lives of the common people. Even the sacred city of Mathurā was not exempt from the iconoclasm of Aurangzib, and there is no evidence that any special school of painting flourished there. However, like Jaipur, it remains one of the chief centers for producing the well-known <term>sāñjhās</term> (paper stencils), examples of which are provided here in Figures 10 and 11; these are used for making floor patterns with colored powders during the Dasehra festival.

Toward the middle of the 18th century, Sikh power began to consolidate in the districts of Amritsar and Jalandhar, and it became established in parts of the hills by the early 19th century. A corresponding group of paintings exists, ranging from about 1750 to 1850, which can be described as the Sikh school. A majority of these are portraits or portrait groups. A fine example expressing true Sikh dignity is reproduced on Plate LXXVI. Many Kāngṛā-Sikh paintings are easily recognized by the fact that the young men in them are clean-shaven—a peculiarity that never appears in Pahāṛī art created for Hindu patrons.¹ An example of this Kāngṛā-Sikh style from the early 19th century is reproduced by Mr. Havell in *Indian Sculpture and Painting*, Plate LXIX. Sikh art is also identifiable in various rather crude "portraits" of the Gurus still produced in Amritsar, and better yet, in some half-obliterated wall-painting fragments about a century old within the precincts of the Golden Temple in Amritsar. It is likely that the Sikhs also occasionally patronized similar work in Kashmir, though I have found little trace of any older or purer tradition there. It may also be mentioned that some copies of the *Granth Sāhib* (the Sikh scripture) are magnificent examples of austere calligraphy, and I have seen one fairly well-illustrated copy said to have been prepared in Kashmir. On the whole, we may say of Sikh painting that while a few distinguished examples exist, the greater part is decadent compared to what came before, whether Rajput or Mughal.

There can be little doubt that Rajput painting, like folk poetry, had definitely passed its peak before the beginning of the 19th century. On the whole, with few exceptions, later Kāngṛā art is to the earlier work what the art of Shāh Jahān was to that of Jahāngīr and Akbar. Still, wise patronage in the 19th century—especially in Jaipur and Kāngṛā—could have preserved much that was worth saving. British occupation always implied the discontinuation of patronage and the more rapid destruction of tradition. However, the vernacular art of Hindustan, which had flourished throughout the Mughal period, was already declining by the time it was first affected by Western influences. These influences never even produced a hybrid official art like some forms of Mughal art, perhaps because the British did not know how to inspire such a thing, or perhaps because art could no longer persist in the shadow of Industrialism. Whatever the case, and even if we excuse the moderns from deliberate destruction, we must admit that Western education, ideals of administrative efficiency, and industrial competition have hastened the end of traditional culture throughout the East—nowhere more conspicuously than in India.

¹ Such as the *Young Warrior* in *Indian Drawings*, I, Plate XIII.

<summary>This page discusses the traditional, recurring nature of Indian art themes, the regional divide between Rajasthan and the Punjab, the emergence of the Sikh school of painting, and the broader decline of traditional artistic patronage under the influence of Western education and industrialization.</summary>

Then both parts of the body moved away from that wound. With such speed of feet and no less diligent effort, as if they were two living beings. Terrified by this miracle, and curious about the cause, we went to the place where I and other pious men were sitting together, and we brought out those pieces which were living vigorously. We were not slightly moved, and we observed them running on the table in whatever direction they could. And if one touched them with a stylus, it would twist itself toward the place of pain, while the other felt nothing and went about its own movements elsewhere. Why say more? We tested how much value this had, and we cut the little worm, or rather, now the little worms, into many parts. They all moved in such a way that, if that had not been done by us and the wounds were not fresh, I would have believed that they had been born whole and separate and had lived each for its own sake. But what I said to those young men then, as they looked at me intently, I fear to say to you now. For we have already proceeded so far that, unless you have something that carries weight for my cause, our great effort, reinforced by such a long discourse, might succumb, having been pierced by a single little worm. I commanded them, however, to keep to their course in their studies just as they had begun, so that they might acquire and learn these things when the opportunity serves, if the matter demands it. But what I discussed with Alipius as they departed, which each of us, according to his own measure, ought to remember, contemplate, and inquire into, if you wish me to explain it, must be said to you at greater length, since it was stated from the very beginning with such mazes and windings. I will not, however, keep silent before you about what I sense, unless many things were already known to me then about the body, about the form that is within the body, about place and time, about motion, which those who say the soul is a body discuss most subtly and abstrusely in order to give the palm to their own side, which I must deflect. For this reason, I warn you again and again, as best I can, not to be rashly swayed either by books or by the disputes of very talkative men who are too excessively attached to the sense of these bodies.

Furthermore, the name of virtue, as well as that of vice, is not used simply, but in many ways. For example, virtue can be a <term>hexis</term> <gloss>disposition/state</gloss> or an <term>energeia</term> <gloss>actuality/action</gloss>. Again, it may be ethical or intellectual. Vice is the same. Moreover, it may be practical or theoretical. The temperate, the just, and the courageous man possess ethical virtues, while the prudent and the wise possess intellectual ones. Again, virtue may be directed toward oneself or toward another. For instance, temperance is directed toward oneself, while justice is directed toward another. For the just man acts justly toward others, whereas the temperate man acts toward himself. Again, virtue may reside in the passion or in the action. For instance, courage resides in the passion, while justice resides in the action. For the courageous man shows courage in the face of fear, while the just man acts justly in his deeds. Again, virtue may be a mean or an extreme. For instance, temperance is a mean, while courage is an extreme. For temperance is the mean between licentiousness and insensitivity, while courage is the extreme between cowardice and recklessness. Again, virtue may be natural or acquired. For instance, temperance may be natural, while justice is acquired. For the temperate person is temperate by nature, but the just person is so by acquisition. Again, virtue may reside in the reason, in the spirit, or in the desire. For instance, prudence resides in the reason, courage in the spirit, and temperance in the desire. For the prudent man thinks with his reason, the courageous man acts with his spirit, and the temperate man governs his desires. Again, virtue may be directed toward God or toward man. For instance, piety is toward God, while justice is toward man. For the pious man is pious toward God, and the just man acts justly toward man. Again, virtue may exist in life or in death. For instance, courage exists in life, while perseverance exists in death. For the courageous man acts in life, while the one who perseveres endures in death. Again, virtue may exist in wealth or in poverty. For instance, liberality exists in wealth, while self-sufficiency exists in poverty. For the liberal man acts liberally in wealth, while the self-sufficient man is content in poverty. Again, virtue may exist in glory or in obscurity. For instance, magnanimity exists in glory, while humility exists in obscurity. For the magnanimous man acts with magnanimity in glory, while the humble man acts with humility in obscurity. Again, virtue may exist in word or in deed. For instance, truth exists in word, while action exists in deed. For the truthful man speaks the truth, and the man of action performs the deed.

<summary>This page categorizes virtue into various types, such as ethical versus intellectual, and explains their manifestations in different aspects of life and action.</summary>
<keywords>virtue, vice, ethical, intellectual, temperance, justice, courage</keywords>

That things indeed did not go smoothly for the Majapahit forces on that campaign is also apparent from the Kidung Sunda fragment mentioned above. As already noted above in Chapter I, this version presumably belongs to the oldest historical traditions, so the information certainly deserves attention. It is told there (cf. above, Chapter III) that the Sundanese <term>patih</term> <gloss>chief minister</gloss> Anepakĕn, in his dispute with Gajah-Mada, demanded that Sunda be treated as an independent kingdom based on recent events. Not only, as Anepakĕn recalled, had Sunda repelled two Javanese attacks, but it had even supported Majapahit when it requested help against Bali through the agency of <term>patih</term> Madhu. ## CAPUT QUADRAGESIMUM SECUNDUM.
### Adulterina. Daun falawar.

**D**aun falawar Conyzæ quoque adfinis videtur, modo autem crefcendi convenit cum Nicotiana anguftifolia. Instar fruticis excrefcit ſtipite lignoſo, fex octove pedes alta, feſeque dividit in plurimos rotundos, & firmos laterales ramos, aliquando quam lattiſſime extenſos inftar arbustulæ.
Folia ſolitaria ſunt, & ſuperius compacta, longiuſculis inſidentia petiolis, anguſtifoliæ Nicotianæ ſimilia, ſed minora, ab utraque parte acuminata, oris æqualibus, ſeptem & novem pollices longa, quatuor & quinque lata, ſed ſuperiora in vetuſtis ſtipitibus minora ſunt, ſuperne intenſe virentia, ſed non ſplendentia, inferne cinerea, ad tactum rugoſa, ac præterea viſcoſa quaſi arena conſperſa, qualis & tota herba eft, ſi quæ conterantur, gravem ſpirant odorem fere inſtar fructus Bate, qui fœtet, ſapor non admodum acris eft, licet ſit amarus & penetrans.
Superiores caules multa gerunt capitula obſcure virentia & arenoſa, in umbellam quaſi collecta, quæ ſeſe aperiunt in floſculos ſordide albicantes, qui inſident calici barbato, & conſtant ex viridi piſtillo, & petalis quinque primo erectis, dein retroflexis cum ſtaminibus brevibus antheras flavas gerentibus, poſt illos fructus excrefcunt rotundi, globulos fclopeti manualis ſeu minoris referentes, arenoſi quoque, primo virides, dein flaveſcentes, intusque repleti granulis planis, in ſuccoſa medulla reconditis.
Folia peculiarem habent characterem, ſed potiſſimum vetuſtiora, quod una nempe ipſorum dimidia pars ad petiolum longior ſit altera. Radix ample diſperſa eft & lignoſa.
*Nomen.* Latine Adulterina, ſive *Folium zelotypiæ*, vel proprie Remedium contra noxam adulterii; Malaice *Daun ſalawar* eadem ſignificatione, Amboinice *Ayloun puti*. *Salawar* autem vocant Malaienſes vitium, quod pueris ſeu infantibus ſupervenit, quum unus parentum, ac præſertim pater adulterii ſit reus, ſeu uxori ſuſpicionem ejus criminis præbet, unde mater ſuſpica & iracunda lac ſuum adulterat, & illud infanti exhibens, ut puto, inde damnum contrahit, mulierculæ enim ſibi perſuadent, infectionem parentis apud alias mulieres contractam, lactantibus ſupervenire, unde hi emaciantur & languent, non autem viris perſuadent, ſimilia vitia ab ipſis peracta infantibus ſuis eſſe noxia.
Nonne hæc juſta est fides, ſeu potius credulitas, quam ſine dubio puto ortam eſſe a quodam genio *Salambar* dicto, quem Arabes & Æthiopes dicunt eſſe diabolum quendam, cujus officium eft ſolum, odium & ſuſpicionem excitare & cauſſare inter nuptos. Qua autem ratione hoc melius peragere is potuit, quam mulierculis perſuadere, ſi infantes ipſarum forte emaciantur, tum parentem adulterii eſſe reum. Hinc rixæ & iræ moventur, unde mox petunt fagas, quæ infantem incantatione, & ſuffimigiis ab hac infectione liberant.
Atque hinc hæc Herba zelotypiæ vocari potest, & genius ſeu Diabolus iſte *Salambar*, dæmon zelotypiæ. Cæterum meliore jure hæc vocatur *Tabaco utan* ſeu *Nicotiana ſylveſtris*, quod nomen huic herbæ magis proprium eft præcedente quarta *Sombong* ſpecie.
*Locus.* Crefcit in gracilibus ſoliis, in locis incultis, in agris, & poſt ædes pagorum.

## TWEE EN VEERTIGSTE HOOFDSTUK.
### *Het Overſpels-kruid.*

**D** *aun falawar wil ook uit de maagfchap van Conyza zyn, dog aan wasdom komt het met den ſmalblaadigen Tabak over een. Het ſchiet op als een heeſter met een houtagtige ſtam, zes en agt voeten hoog, die zig in veele ronde en ſtyve zydetakken verdeeld, zomtyds zeer wyd uitgebreid als een formeel boompje.*
*De bladeren ſtaan enkeld, en na vooren toe digt op malkander op langagtige ſteelen, den ſmalblaadige Tabak gelyk, dog kleinder, agter en vooren toegeſpitst, met evene kanten, zeven en negen duimen lang, vier en vyf breed, dog de voorſte aan de oude ſtokken zyn kleinder, boven hoog-groen, dog doods, van onderen wat graauw, ruig in 't aantaſten, en daar en boven met een kleeverig zand bestrooit, gelyk ook 't geheele kruid is, als men ze wryft, van een zwaaren reuk, ſchier als de vrugten van Bate die ſtinken, de ſmaak is niet zonderlyk ſcherp, hoewel wat bitter en doordringende.*
*De bovenſte ſteelen dragen veele doods-groene en zandige knopjes by een gehoopt in een dolle, waar uit werden kleine vuil-witte bloempjes, met een groen middel-ribbetje van vyf overeind ſtaande, daar na agterwaarts gebooge blaadjes gemaakt, in een diep geboord kelkje, in de midden met korte draadjes, en daar op veele geele noppen met nog een langer ſtyltje bloed, na dezelven volgen ronde vrugten als Piſtool-kogels mede zandig, eerſt groen, daar na bleek-geel, binnen vol kleine platte korrels in een fappig merg.*
*De bladeren hebben tot een byzonder merkteken, dog meeſt de oude, dat zy de eene zyde agter aan den ſteel langer hebben als de andere. De wortel is wyd verſpreid, en houtagtig.*
*Naam. In 't Latyn Adulterina; ſive Folium zelotypiæ; of eigentlyk Remedium contra noxam adulterii; in 't Maleits Daun falawar met dezelve beduidenisſe; in 't Amboins Ayloun puti. Salawar nu noemen de Maleiers het kwaad, dat de kleine kinderen over komt, als een van de ouders, inzonderheid de vader zig in overſpel verloopt, of immers de moeder ſuſpicii daar toe geeft, waar door de jaloeze moeder ontſteeken zynde met haar zog, zoo ik gisſe, het kind ook ontſtelt, want de vrouwtjes maken 't malkanderen zoo wys, dat de ſmettinge door den vader by andere vrouwen bebaald, aan de zuigende kinderen overgaat, waar door dezelve ongedaan, mager en ziekelyk werden, maar zy willen de mannen niet wyzer maken, dat diergelyke fouten by haar begaan, baare kinderen ſchadelyk zy.*
*Is dat niet een fraay geloove, 't welk ik vaſtelyk ſuſtineer zyn oorſpronk te hebben van een zeker geeft Salambar genoemd, den welken de Arabiers, en Mooren zeggen een duivel te zyn, wiens werk en officie anders niet is dan haat en jaloezy tusſen getrouwde lieden te verwekken. ## CHAPTER FORTY-TWO.
### The Adulteress Herb. Daun falawar.

**D**aun falawar also seems related to the Conyza, yet in its manner of growth it resembles narrow-leaved Tobacco. It grows like a shrub with a woody stem, six or eight feet high, and divides into many round and firm side branches, sometimes spreading as wide as a small tree.
The leaves are solitary and clustered at the top, sitting on rather long stalks; they are similar to narrow-leaved Tobacco but smaller, pointed at both ends, with even edges, seven to nine inches long and four to five wide. However, the upper leaves on older stems are smaller. They are deep green above but not shiny, and ash-colored below, rough to the touch and moreover viscous as if sprinkled with sand—as is the whole herb. If crushed, they give off a heavy odor much like the stinking Bate fruit <note>original: "fructus Bate"; likely referring to a local fruit known for a pungent, perhaps cadaverous, smell</note>; the taste is not particularly sharp, though it is bitter and penetrating.
The upper stalks bear many dull green and sandy little heads clustered together like an umbrella, which open into small, dirty white flowers. These sit in a bearded cup <note>original: "calici barbato"; the calyx of the flower</note> and consist of a green pistil and five petals, which are at first erect and then bent backward, with short filaments bearing yellow anthers. After these, round fruits grow out, resembling the balls of a pistol or small handgun, also sandy, first green and then yellowish, filled inside with flat grains hidden in a juicy pith.
The leaves have a peculiar characteristic, especially the older ones, in that one half of the leaf at the stalk is longer than the other. The root is widely spread and woody.
*Name.* In Latin, *Adulterina* <note>original: "Adulterina"; meaning 'The Adulteress'</note>, or *Folium zelotypiae* <note>original: "Leaf of Jealousy"</note>, or more properly, a remedy against the harm of adultery. In Malay, *Daun salawar* has the same meaning, and in Amboinese, *Ayloun puti*. Now, the Malays use the term *Salawar* for an affliction that comes upon young children or infants when one of the parents, especially the father, is guilty of adultery, or at least gives the wife cause for suspicion of that crime. Because of this, the suspicious and angry mother "adulterates" her milk, and by giving it to the infant, as I believe, causes harm. For the common women convince one another that the infection contracted by the parent with other women passes to the nursing children, whereby they become emaciated and languid. However, they do not convince the men that such faults committed by them are harmful to their children.
Is this not a fine faith, or rather a credulity, which I firmly believe arose from a certain spirit called *Salambar*, whom the Arabs and Ethiopians say is a certain devil whose only duty and office is to stir up and cause hatred and suspicion between married people? How could he accomplish this better than by persuading the women that if their infants happen to grow thin and sickly, the father must have been unfaithful? <note>Dutch original: "buiten de pot gepist"; literally "pissed outside the pot," a common idiom for cheating or adultery</note> From this, quarrels and anger are stirred up, whereupon they immediately seek out witches who free the infant from this infection with incantations and fumigations.
And for this reason, this herb can be called the Herb of Jealousy, and that spirit or devil *Salambar*, the demon of jealousy. Otherwise, it is called with better reason *Tabaco utan* or Wild Tobacco, which name is more proper to this herb than to the preceding fourth species of *Sombong*.
*Location.* It grows on thin soils, in uncultivated places, in fields, and behind the houses of the villages <term>Negorijen: native villages or settlements in the Dutch East Indies</term>.

## FORTY-SECOND CHAPTER.
### *The Adultery Herb.*

**D** *aun falawar also belongs to the family of Conyza, yet in its manner of growth it agrees with the narrow-leaved Tobacco. It shoots up as a shrub with a woody stem, six and eight feet high, which divides into many round and stiff side branches, sometimes very widely spread like a formal little tree.*
*The leaves stand singly, and toward the front they are close together on somewhat long stalks, like the narrow-leaved Tobacco, though smaller, pointed at the back and front, with even edges, seven and nine inches long, four and five wide, though the front ones on the old stalks are smaller. They are deep green above, but dull, somewhat gray from beneath, rough to the touch, and moreover sprinkled with a sticky sand, just as the whole herb is. When one rubs them, they have a heavy smell, almost like the fruits of Bate that stink; the taste is not particularly sharp, although somewhat bitter and penetrating.*
*The uppermost stalks bear many dull green and sandy buds heaped together in a cluster, from which are made small dirty-white flowers, with a green mid-rib, of five standing upright, then backward-bent petals, in a deep-bored little cup. In the middle are short threads, and upon them many yellow nubs with another longer style; after these follow round fruits like pistol balls, also sandy, first green, thereafter pale yellow, inside full of small flat grains in a juicy pith.*
*The leaves have as a particular mark, though mostly the old ones, that they have one side at the back of the stalk longer than the other. The root is widely spread and woody.*
*Name. In Latin Adulterina; or Leaf of Jealousy; or properly Remedy against the harm of adultery; in Malay Daun salawar with the same meaning; in Amboinese Ayloun puti. Salawar is what the Malays call the evil that happens to small children when one of the parents, especially the father, strays into adultery, or at least gives the mother suspicion thereof. Through this, the jealous mother being inflamed, she also upsets the child with her milk, as I guess. For the women make each other so wise as to believe that the infection caught by the father from other women passes to the nursing children, whereby they become undone, thin, and sickly. But they do not want to make the men any wiser, that such faults committed by them are harmful to their children.*
*Is that not a fine belief, which I firmly maintain has its origin from a certain spirit called Salambar, whom the Arabs and Moors say is a devil, whose work and office is nothing other than to provoke hatred and jealousy between married people. And how could he have done this better than to make the women believe that when their children by chance become thin and sickly, the father must have "pissed outside the pot" <note>original: "buiten de pot gepist"; unfaithful</note>. Then it first comes to a raging and storming, and then one runs immediately to an old witch, who frees the child from this infection with fumigation and incantations.*
*For this reason, one may call this herb the Herb of Jealousy, and the aforementioned Spirit Salambar, the demon of jealousy. Otherwise, one calls it with better reason also Tabaco utan, or wild Tobacco, which name is more proper to this herb than the preceding fourth sort of Sombong.*
*Place. It grows on lean soils, uncultivated places in the field, and behind the houses of the villages.*

# On Open Sores / The First Book

<margin>A</margin>Does this, however, concern the elements? If everything were made only of elements, then nothing on Earth would be perishable. It is indeed true that the body has the four elements within it—warmth and cold—at least in healthy things. But when health is broken, the element is no longer there; heat and cold depart. Whatever is thus displaced from the element belongs to death. The warmth and cold in the body that a human requires for life is the <term>Element of Fire</term> <note>original: "Elementum Ignis"</note>. But when speaking of diseases, all of that must be set aside. Flesh that is attacked by <term>corrosives</term> <note>substances that eat away at body tissue</note> is still part of the living; but once it is separated and falls away, it becomes that which you [traditional doctors] mistakenly believe still stands as part of the body. Now, if its place is filled with other flesh, as the Creator ordained, that new growth is no longer "flesh" in the same sense, because it no longer possesses that elemental warmth. For whatever is pulled or made outside of the natural seed has no element dwelling within it. The warmth it does have is borrowed from the healthy flesh in its neighborhood. It is just like a <term>grain sack</term> <note>original: "Krisensack," a bag filled with grain or herbs used as a heat compress</note> that becomes warm behind the stove; it is a borrowed warmth from the fire inside the stove. So it is with these dead things; they only have a resemblance to life in which they maintain themselves. 

But to speak further of the heat of disease, or its cold—from whence they come—it is partly borrowed from <term>exertion</term> <note>original: "Exercitation"</note>, like one who sweats from labor. Similarly, <term>obstructions</term> <note>original: "Oppilationen," blockages of the body's vessels or pores</note> prevent an exit and cause a buildup, like dammed-up water. These are all "foreign" heats, in which neither the <term>complexions</term> <note>the traditional four temperaments: sanguine, choleric, melancholic, and phlegmatic</note> nor the elements have anything to do. And note this as well: if such heat or cold were to come from the complexion, it would be possible for you to mutate the complexions as you pleased. If you could break a heat, you could create a cold, and conversely <note>original: "per contrarium"</note>. But it is just as in <term>putrefactions</term> <note>original: "Putrefactionibus," the process of decay or fermentation</note>—that is, a manure pile that lies together and is laid down cold; it has a nature within it that makes it become hotter than when it first came out of the horse's belly. And though it becomes ever so hot, it is still not an element, nor is it the "complexion" of the manure; it is a product of <term>digestion</term> <note>here meaning fermentation or internal chemical ripening</note>.

<margin>B</margin>All of this is merely a beginning of knowledge, leading to a greater understanding and a foundation for the theory of error and the process of open sores.

Note also that in Nature there are many such examples that might give "degrees" to a simple physician. Take <term>salts</term> <note>original: "Salibus"</note>, for example: they have a common element, but they accomplish nothing through that element. We cannot use or administer an element, for they are clear in their <term>virtues</term> <note>original: "Virtutibus," the specific healing powers or inherent properties of a substance</note>; they live from them alone and act from them alone. As for the further distinctions—such as <term>sal ammoniac</term> <note>original: "Salmiar"</note> compared to <term>sea salt</term> <note>original: "Sal maris"</note>, or <term>rock alum</term> <note>original: "Alumen rochum"</note> compared to <term>feather alum</term> <note>original: "Plumolum," likely a form of asbestos or fibrous alum</note>—this is not the fault of the elements. It is the fault of the Power, which is sour or sweet, sharp or salty; yet one has just as much of the element as the other. Therefore, <term>saltiness</term>, <term>bitterness</term>, <term>sweetness</term>, <term>harshness</term>, <term>roughness</term>, <term>sourness</term>, etc., should be attributed to that specific nature and not to other things; nor should one estimate a "complexion" to be higher or lower because of them. Such a nature is just as one human is distinguished from another by beauty or strength, which is not a property of the elements; likewise, the essence of <term>salts</term> <note>original: "Salia"</note> is a specific nature. Thus, <term>rock salt</term> <note>original: "Sal Gemmæ"</note> is sharper than <term>natron</term> <note>original: "Sal Anathron," an Egyptian salt/soda</note>, just as one human is sharper than another, and all of this is outside of the complexion. Just as one sharp tongue cuts more than another, yet they are all fleshy and of one form. And as rock salt is "prettier" than natron, it must also be more transparent and sharper. For beauty gives the <term>exaltation</term> <note>the refinement or heightening of a substance's properties</note> of the nature and virtue to the body, and not to the element. And as sal ammoniac is stronger than sea salt, that is the fault of "Strength," just as one man is stronger than another. Now look at where that strength comes from: for just as it is greater in one than in another, so also is the sharpness and piquancy greater in one than in another. The cold in <term>camphor</term> <note>original: "Gampffer"</note> is not of the element; it belongs to its specific nature, and it has not a speck more [of the element of water] than warm water does. Likewise, <term>Spanish flies</term> <note>original: "Cantharides," beetles used to create medicinal blisters</note> burn blisters, but not by the power of the element of Fire! For they have not a speck more of it than <term>chamomile</term> <note>original: "Camillen"</note> does. <term>Nettles</term> <note>original: "Nestlen"</note> also burn, not because of the element of Fire, but because of the subtlety of their form, which is their nature.

<margin>C</margin>These are <term>mysteries</term> <note>original: "Mysteria"</note> and <term>great works</term> <note>original: "Magnalia"</note> thus ordained by God above the elements and complexions. And whatever burns, bites, eats away, etc., is as closely attached to the "complexion" as a word is to the mouth [that speaks it]. For just as a word is not made of elements, neither are the nature and <term>natural virtues</term> <note>original: "virtutes naturalium"</note> of the elements. And if you undertake <term>philosophy</term> <note>here meaning the study of nature</note> with a correct foundation, your diseases will be seen to have a free origin, and not be like a <term>weaver’s pattern</term> <note>original: "Weberzettel," implying a rigid, predetermined structure</note>. Although you have not thought of such a foundation yourselves, it comes to you from those "philosophers" who should in no way be used in medicine with such errors and poorly-founded "doctoring." For <term>Aristotle</term>, <term>Averroes</term>, <term>Albertus</term>, and others will have no seat in such <term>natural sciences</term> <note>original: "Naturalibus"</note>, for they were not entrusted with medicine, so that they should be upheld with such authority. You know that the teachings of the philosophers and their like are set down in books without any experience, which should in no way have a place or position in medicine.

Hinc uulgus nostrum sua consuetudine linguam cerui uocat hemionium. ### Dracunculus. Chapter XCVI

The greater *Dracunculus*, as Dioscorides left witnessed, grows in shaded places and around fences, with a smooth and glabrous stalk, straight, two cubits high, the thickness of a staff, with the variegated spots of dragons, distinguished by numerous purple markings, with leaves like sorrel, opposite in mutual embrace. It makes a fruit at the top of the stalk, racemose, of a color between gray at the beginning, later when it has ripened, blushing with saffron and crimson, with a large, white, round root, covered with a thin bark. It is gathered when it blackens with maturity. But this seems to me supposititious, especially since both Galen and Paul, who are accustomed to report the sayings of this author in good faith, make mention of only one *dracunculus*. The suspicion was also increased that no trace of this drawing is shown among the ancients, who everywhere adhered to the tenets of Dioscorides; and if the most ancient codices are consulted, they will finally be found to have noted no difference between the lesser and greater *dracunculus*. But which will be called the lesser, when a height of two cubits is assigned to the stalk of each? Wherefore, we suspect that the chapter which is dedicated to the greater *dracunculus* has accrued to the history of Dioscorides, especially since both claim the same appearance, size, habit, variegated skin, and native places for themselves. For both grow in shaded places around hedges and thickets, with a round root clothed in a thin bark, a straight stalk, two cubits high, the thickness of a staff, with the variegated spots of snakes, with purple markings intervening, with fruit in a raceme at the summit, the berries first green in pallor; wherefore in one it is read as gray, in the other as herbaceous. Which, when they have ripened, blush with the color of saffron or crimson. But what would trouble the reader most of all is that they seem to differ much in the leaves; in one they are designated as sorrel, in the other as ivy-like. But they exit into much more distant angles, nor are they rounded with the legitimate compass of ivy. Dioscorides explained the appearance of this leaf in his mention of *hemionium*. For he represented *hemionium* with the leaf of *dracunculus*, which is very long and almost the shape of sorrel. Hence our common people, by their custom, call *hemionium* the tongue of the deer. Wherefore, so that all suspicion may depart, we believe there is only one genus of *dracunculus*, represented by a double history, yet we judge the former to have been an addition, and to have emerged from the workshop not of Dioscorides, but of another author. Add that the virtues, even if they are described with various words, are found not to be much different or abhorrent from one another. In our region, it is found frequently enough, and is studiously cultivated in gardens, a miracle of a playful nature, and of a dragon learning to make rudiments in plants. *Dracunculus* rises with a simple stalk, two cubits high, smooth and glabrous, the thickness of a staff, variegated with the colored spots of snakes, with purple markings also intervening, so that it clearly seems to feign the habit and color of a serpent. At the leafy summit, leaves emerge, six or seven in number, hanging down like fingers on a thick petiole, sprinkled with whitish marks, of the shape of sorrel, but of a longer, ivy-like appearance. From the leafy top of the scape, a certain sheath emerges, herbaceous on the outside, almost a cubit in length, gradually tapering to a point, as if it were an involucrum for a birth about to erupt, which, when it splits and unfolds itself, shows a purple horn tapered to a point. Distended by the growth of the seeds, it splits into a fissure, and finally, weakening, it grows flaccid, and dries up and perishes, leaving the horn. The racemose fruit surrounds its lower part, with berries green in their first maturity, and reddening with the color of kermes during their youth, with a biting taste and a rank odor, as long as it puts forth that violet-colored horn; with a bulbous root, clothed in a thin bark. It grows in shaded hedges. But it is now also sown in gardens, in the spectacular form of a gaping dragon, with a solid horn appearing as if it were a tongue, and the concave hollow of the sheath like the maw of a serpent. Nor can anyone deny that this is the herb which the apothecaries call *serpentaria*. For among the ancient Romans, the use of the name *colubrina* and *serpentaria* had become common, nor could a more apt word be used for it, since the smooth stalk, sprinkled with purple marks, represents and equals the body of a snake in its variegated appearance and length, and the summit, also with the winding maw of the mouth, expresses a head protruding a bloody tongue. *Dracunculus* is shown by Pliny in triple form: with leaves of beet, not without a thyrsus, and a purple flower; this, as he says, is similar to *arum*.
